content: Chief of nuclear watchdog says secret Assad-era facility would have been able to produce fissile material A nearly complete nuclear reactor built secretly during the rule of the toppled Syrian leader Bashar al-Assad would have been able to produce fissile material for possible use in nuclear weapons, the chief of the UN nuclear watchdog has revealed. Inspectors from the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) last month visited two sites, one in Deir ez-Zor and a second in an undisclosed location identified to them by Syrian authorities. Continue reading...
title: Syrian reactor could have been used for nuclear weapons if completed, UN says
author: Guardian staff and agencies in Vienna

content: Stuart Reges, a University of Washington (UW) computer science professor who in 2022 was reprimanded and investigated for mocking a "land acknowledgment," last week received $600,000 as part of an agreement that settles the ensuing First Amendment lawsuit . But Reges did not get an apology or an admission of wrongdoing from the Seattle university, whose spokesman still insists that "we acted appropriately." The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit disagreed last December, when a divided three-judge panel ruled that UW administrators violated Reges' First Amendment rights by subjecting him to an inquisition that lasted nearly a year, during which he was denied a merit pay increase, based on his alleged violation of the university's vague "antiharassment" policy. According to the 9th Circuit's decision in Reges v. Cauce , the state university retaliated against Reges for protected speech and engaged in viewpoint discrimination, which is presumptively unconstitutional . "They broke the law, but refuse to admit it," Reges writes in the New York Post . "I am astonished that the university still insists that it behaved appropriately." The UW investigation was prompted by a statement that Reges included in the syllabus for the introductory computer science course he has taught for more than two decades: "I acknowledge that by the labor theory of property the Coast Salish people can claim historical ownership of almost none of the land currently occupied by the University of Washington." Reges, a critic of "diversity, equity, and inclusion" (DEI) policies, was alluding to John Locke while making fun of a university-recommended syllabus statement that "acknowledges the Coast Salish peoples of this land, the land which touches the shared waters of all tribes and bands within the Suquamish, Tulalip and Muckleshoot nations." Reges saw the land acknowledgment as part of a DEI agenda that "treats some groups of students as more deserving of recognition and welcome than others on account of their race or other immutable characteristic." He thought it was inappropriate to include such a "political statement" in his syllabus and questioned its factual premise, noting that "most of the land currently occupied by UW was densely forested before the land was cleared to make way for the campus." He objected to the implication that "UW's presence is somehow illegitimate, shameful, morally wrong, or unlawful," and deemed the recommended statement "an empty, performative act of moralism." UW administrators viewed Reges' dissent as intolerable, saying it had caused unacceptable "disruption" at the university. The 9th Circuit did not buy it. "Student discomfort with a professor's views can prompt discussion and disapproval," Judge Daniel A. Bress, a Donald Trump appointee, wrote in an opinion joined by Judge Milan D. Smith Jr., who was nominated by George W. Bush. "But this discomfort is not grounds for the university retaliating against the professor. We hold that th
title: Professor Investigated for Mocking a University 'Land Acknowledgment' Gets a $600,000 Settlement
author: Jacob Sullum

content: The ancient Greeks had three distinct words for anger. Until “Furious,” I had no idea this was the case – but then, I’m not a “nut about mythology,” as FBI agent Nora Washington (Quincy Tyler Bernstine) describes herself. Nora explains to the counselor running a workplace mental health seminar that the Greeks viewed anger as a kind of insanity, but with different diagnostic profiles. There’s Mênis, which Nora defines as the anger of a society or a people. Thumos is the hero’s anger, goading a person to fight or kill. Then, she says with special relish, there’s Orge, pronounced or-gay . “That’s the slow, quiet anger that builds up in you, until you finally decide to do something about it,” she says. Orge, you can tell from Nora’s viperish grin as she stares down her unctuous supervisor, Ed George (Danny McCarthy), is her favorite. It’s rare in these days of the Netflix exposition dump for a show to explain what it’s all about in concise moments like this. “Furious,” created by Liz Meriwether , is full of them. Every time we see Nora, we get a sense of how long she’s been carrying her anger without her saying so. She’s more than a little too partial to hard liquor, but if her orge started as cheap wine, it is now a richly aged vinegar eating away at her stomach lining. (Disney/Sarah Shatz) Emily Rossum and Quincy Tyler Bernstine in “Furious” Nora is the tertiary protagonist of “Furious.” Emmy Rossum ’s Alice Black is its main hero, a recently arrived FBI employee dismissed by her more experienced male peers as a “baby agent.” But Alice was once a detective for the NYPD, yanked back there when her former partner Danny Kelly ( Scoot McNairy ) calls her to consult on the murder of a powerful man’s son.  Soon Alice and Danny connect the victim’s father to a conspiracy akin to the one that made Jeffrey Epstein a household name. By then we’ve also met the killer: Catherine Grace ( Lola Petticrew ), a girlish waif who carries her mortal devices inside a sparkly purse. Catherine is a damaged creature, but so is Alice, whose boyfriend, a fellow cop (played by Jake Lacy ), used to drag her out of the shower to pummel her unconscious. A common trait of trauma survivors is being stuck in a behavioral loop associated with their mistreatment. Alice works to be unreadable, a gray rock who in her free time finds guys on dating apps to beat her up as sexual foreplay. Catherine is a chimeric contortion of an ice-cold seductress and a deceitful teenage cherub, which is around the age she got lost. Add in Nora, an emotionally ground-down FBI veteran who wrangles Alice onto her team, which investigates horror acts nobody else wants to look at — sex crimes and crimes against children — and you have an accurate, modern rendering of the Erinyes, a triune team older than the gods themselves. The poet Virgil named them as Alecto, Megaera and Tisiphone. The Romans dubbed them the Furies.   Related Welcome to bee season! Women are furious, but you
title: Women’s rage is in season again
author: Melanie McFarland

content: O ne simple rule shapes Kansas politics: Republicans win statewide. In U.S. Senate races, the GOP has prevailed without interruption for more than 90 years. But the rule has a corollary, which accounts for the occasional Democratic governor. A Republican thought to be too extreme, too ideological, or too big for their britches can be beaten by a centrist Democrat when the wind blows just right. And so, on the same August Tuesday that saw Michigan Democrats choose Abdul El-Sayed, Kansas Republicans realized their safe seat might not be so safe. Kansas Democrats had picked a man who extols moderation as a matter of faith—literally. Adam Hamilton, the founding pastor of America’s largest mainline Protestant congregation, will challenge the first-term incumbent Senator Roger Marshall in November. In the handful of months since he announced his candidacy, Hamilton has defeated 10 garden-variety Democrats in the primary while setting new records for Kansas fundraising, pulling in $1 million in his first week and nearly $3.7 million in his first quarter. Political analysts continue to rate Hamilton a long shot; admittedly, they have nine decades of justification. But Marshall ticks every box that can mean trouble for otherwise-invulnerable Kansas Republicans. Full of himself even by senatorial standards (one Republican Senate colleague described him to me as a “know-it-all”), Marshall is leery of public forums where he might hear from protesters and tends to speak before thinking—a hazard of his appetite for cable-TV appearances. In nearly six years as a constituent of the senator, I have traveled from one end of Kansas to the other, and I have concluded that passionate supporters of Roger Marshall are the electoral equivalent of jackalopes: If they exist, I have never found one. Should Hamilton break the Senate’s longest GOP win streak, he would score more than an enormous off-year upset; his influence on 2028—a free-for-all to define post–Donald Trump politics—could be even larger. Because Hamilton seeks to vindicate the belief, beleaguered in today’s culture, that moderation is a good thing, not just as an electoral strategy, but as an approach to life. [ Elizabeth Bruenig: Texans will decide if Jesus was a lefty ] In Texas, James Talarico’s Christianity seems, at times, to dovetail with uncanny precision with the agenda of secular progressivism. Hamilton’s rhetoric suggests that his Democratic revival tent would be roomier, but at the same time he has so far faced relatively little pressure to translate his disposition into details. He is motivated by “compassion, a belief in safety nets for vulnerable people,” he told me, and also by “fiscal responsibility, limited government, and strong defense.” Such inoffensive straddling may be out of step with today’s politics. “People are really pissing mad, really, really pissing mad,” El-Sayed explained to Michelle Goldberg of The New York Times . A roiling left has risen to match Trump’s raging right. To w
title: What’s the Matter With Moderation?
author: David Von Drehle

content: Jon Ronson had never really thought about the term masculinity until a strange series of events led him down a rabbit hole involving castles, cage fights, and an actor playing a horse. Host Charlie Warzel talks to Ronson about the disinhibited men who are looking for purpose in all the wrong places. Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube The following is a transcript of the episode: Jon Ronson: So I think, beginning with deindustrialization, the death of factories, office life eroding, men realizing that certain privileges they had they don’t quite have the same way anymore—feeling kind of tossed around in a sea of conflicting ideologies about what being a man actually means. Should you be more stoical? Should you be more vulnerable? You know, all of these men’s-health influencers giving these differing, contrasting ideas. And so this is a huge societal shift in many different ways. And I think that’s what’s happening. You’ve got men responding to these changes by bowing out, and then you’ve got these other men who are responding by spiraling. Charlie Warzel: I’m Charlie Warzel, and this is Galaxy Brain , and today we are headed down a rabbit hole that includes ominous castles, public shaming, YouTube, White House cage fighting, all to answer one of life’s burning questions. Why is it that so many men are unraveling these days? Is this part of a changing economy? Part of a bad job market? Is it fallout from the pandemic? Or, is it part of something bigger? A societal failure of some sort, or an outgrowth of what some people have called the masculinity crisis? Now those words, masculinity crisis , can cause some people to roll their eyes. Men, of course, continue to enjoy all kinds of societal privilege, and gender inequities abound. But what is clear, I think, if you spent any time engaging with modern politics and culture, is that over the last few decades there has been a very real, if hard to define, debate over what it means to be a man. Jobs and gender roles—they’ve changed, and culture along with it. Much of it for the better. But that change has also created some uncertainty for the men who have been used to being at the center of every household, every office, every institution, marketing campaign, and political decision. And it’s in that uncertainty that all kinds of voices, pickup artists, politicians, incels on 4chan, Andrew Tate, Jordan Peterson—you name it—they’ve all jumped in to offer these competing visions of masculinity. Now, some of this has taken the form of toxic, misogynistic, manosphere bullshit. Some of it is just positive or harmless—“dudes rock” kind of stuff. And so many of these lessons, they end up being taught or absorbed, for better or for worse, in online communities and communicated by people who may or may not have ulterior motives. So what happens to regular men in this bizarre online stew that we’re all in? My guest today, the writer and podcaster Jon Ronson, explores that in his new book, The Castl
title: Why So Many Men Are Unraveling
author: Charlie Warzel
